summary: A 1980 revision of the Internet Message Protocol, which describes a way to send messages between hosts. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A set of rules for passing messages between computers on connected networks, now no longer used.

subtitle: A comprehensive protocol for transmitting messages and multimedia between networked computers.

tldr.problem: Early message systems in the ARPANET operated independently with different formats and capabilities. A unified, internetwork message protocol was needed to allow different networks to exchange messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 759 defines the Internet Message Protocol, implemented in Message Processing Modules (MPMs) that exchange messages containing an identification, a command for routing, and a document that can include text, graphics, facsimile, or voice.
tldr.outcome: This protocol is now historic and has been superseded by SMTP and related standards, but it pioneered the concept of structured multimedia messages in email.

today: RFC 759 is Historic and has been superseded by SMTP (RFC 5321) and related standards. However, it pioneered the concept of structured multimedia messages and a modular approach to message routing that influenced later email system designs.

sections.title: Internetwork Message Systems
sections.content:
RFC 759 describes a system for transmitting messages between Message Processing Modules (MPMs) running on host computers in different networks. The system is designed for the ARPA internetwork environment where networks are connected through gateways, but is general enough for any interconnected system.

The key innovation is support for multimedia messages. Rather than text only, messages can include data objects representing drawings, facsimile images, or digitized speech. An MPM can be implemented in any network and will interoperate with MPMs in other networks through a standard protocol.
sections.eli5: An MPM is like a post office for computers. Different post offices on different networks can send mail to each other, and the mail can contain pictures and voice, not just text.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
Every message consists of three parts: a transaction identifier that uniquely identifies the message, a command containing routing information (network, host, user, protocol), and a document with optional header fields and a body. The body can be simple text or a complex structure containing multimedia data with controlled presentation: sequential (one after another), simultaneous (at the same time), or independent (in any order).

For conversion between local mail systems and the internet message format, special transformation programs are required. When an internet message with mixed media must be delivered to a system that only supports text, the non-text content may be summarized or discarded to preserve as much information as possible.
sections.eli5: Each message has an ID (so you know which one it is), directions (where it goes), and the content (which can be text, pictures, sound, or mixed).

sections.title: Routing and Delivery
sections.content:
An MPM discovers unprocessed input, examines its destination, and routes it using routing tables. Delivery can be to another user on the same host, a user on the same network, or a user on another network. For same-network delivery, the MPM sends directly to that host. For other-network delivery, the MPM sends either directly to a known MPM in the destination network, or to a nearby MPM that has broader knowledge of the internet for relay.

Different networks may have their own message systems. In that case, an intra-network message uses the local system, while inter-network messages pass through the internet message system via MPMs and gateways.
sections.eli5: If the mail is for someone here, put it in their mailbox. If it is for another computer, send it there. If you do not know how to reach that computer, send it to a big mail hub that does.

sections.title: System Interfaces
sections.content:
The MPM uses a reliable communication service, typically the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), to communicate with other MPMs. This service provides bidirectional logical connections, commands to open and close connections, and flow control. The MPM receives input from User Interface Programs (UIPs) and data structures, and produces output in data structures that UIPs and other programs consume.

The message itself is represented as a structured data object with typed data elements. Internally within an MPM or UIP, a message may be represented in any convenient form, but when transmitted between MPMs or exchanged with a UIP, it uses the standard structured format.
sections.eli5: The MPM talks to other MPMs using TCP (a reliable communication method). UIPs (user programs) create messages and read received messages by putting data into shared structures.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", RFC 793, September 1981.
